The graduation party at Tuan's parents' house in Melbourne was loud: aunties, cousins, a huge tray of spring rolls, and a banner his mother had printed: FIRST CLASS HONOURS! ACCOUNTING!
Tuan smiled for every photo. It was the result his dad had talked about since Tuan was fourteen, and he'd hit it exactly.
Later, Daniel found him on the back step, a plate going cold on his knees.
'You did it, man. Why do you look like you lost something?'
Tuan turned the paper plate slowly. 'I kept thinking that when I got here, I'd feel... done. Happy. I just feel like I finished someone else's homework.'
Inside, his dad was telling the story of the results email for the third time.
'What would have felt like yours?' Daniel asked.
Tuan didn't answer. He was looking at the vegetable garden he'd been planting with his grandmother every weekend for years.

qa.q: What did the banner Tuan's mother printed say?
qa.a: FIRST CLASS HONOURS! ACCOUNTING!

qa.q: Why does Tuan feel empty after reaching the goal?
qa.a: The target had been his dad's since Tuan was fourteen, not something he valued himself; reaching it felt like finishing 'someone else's homework'.

qa.q: What question could become a turning point for Tuan, and why?
qa.a: Daniel's 'What would have felt like yours?'; it invites Tuan to look at his own values, perhaps the garden he tends with his grandmother, instead of borrowed targets.

qa.q: How might Tuan's dad see the day, compared with Tuan?
qa.a: His dad is proud and happy, retelling the results email; he probably has no idea Tuan feels empty, since to him the goal was a gift.

grounding: A young man reaches the degree result his family set for him and feels empty, because the goal was never his own.

The hostel common room at the engineering college erupted when the warden read out the result: 'General Secretary, Jatin Rathore, 212 votes.' Jatin's wing lifted him onto their shoulders, chanting.
It had been Ramesh's idea since first year. 'You'll be GS, bro. Our wing needs a GS.' Ramesh made the posters, planned the speeches and counted votes in his head for weeks.
That night, after the sweets and the selfies, Jatin sat alone in the empty mess, the victory garland on the table beside him.
He had wanted this, hadn't he? He'd said so a hundred times. So why did it feel like a costume?
What he had really enjoyed all year was Saturday evenings teaching maths to the canteen workers' children, which nobody had voted for.
Ramesh came in. 'GS! Why are you sitting here in the dark?'

qa.q: How many votes did Jatin get?
qa.a: 212 votes.

qa.q: Why did the win feel like a costume to Jatin?
qa.a: The goal came from Ramesh and the wing, not from what Jatin valued; he had said he wanted it so often that he never checked, and reaching it left him empty.

qa.q: What choice could Jatin make now that he has noticed where he felt most alive?
qa.a: Jatin could put real energy into the Saturday maths classes, perhaps using the post to support them; linking the role to what he values might make it feel like his own.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel on finding Jatin alone in the dark?
qa.a: Ramesh, who worked for years on this win, would likely be confused and a little hurt, not realising the goal was mostly his own.

grounding: A student wins a hostel election his friends set as his goal and feels hollow, since his real interest lay elsewhere.

Dear Ujjwal,
You asked how the book is going. Here's the honest version.
Big aim: finish my Urdu picture book about the kite-seller and send it to three publishers by December.
Monthly: March, the story. April and May, twelve sketches. June, final text. And so on.
Weekly: two sketches and one page of text, every Sunday morning with chai.
Every Sunday night I look back at the week. Not to scold myself. Just: what got done, what didn't, what changes. Two weeks ago Ammi was unwell and I did nothing at all. Old me would have given up. Instead I wrote 'Missed. Fine. Move April's sketches into May.' And carried on.
I'm on sketch nine now. It might be a month late. It's still going to happen.
Come and meet the kite-seller when you visit.
Parveen

Bhavna, you asked how I switched from data entry to a design job in one year. There's no trick. There's a notebook.
Page one: 'Junior designer job by next March.' Big and scary.
Page two, I broke it down. Months one to three: basics from a free course. Four to six: three practice projects. Seven to nine: portfolio and feedback. Ten to twelve: apply everywhere.
Then the weeks. Every Monday I wrote three small tasks. Watch two lessons. Redesign one app screen. Ask one person for feedback.
Every Sunday I sat with the notebook and reviewed the week kindly, the way a friend would. In July I fell sick and lost three weeks. I didn't tear up the plan. I just pushed the portfolio back a month.
The offer came in April, not March. Close enough. The Minakshi who wrote page one only had to keep turning pages.

qa.a: Pushed the portfolio stage back a month instead of tearing up the plan; that flexibility let the big aim survive real life, and the offer still came in April.

Last August I lost the zonal debate. Not just lost: I blanked on my rebuttal, stood there for eight seconds, and someone at the back laughed. Vaibhav, my partner, had to finish for me.
After that, something shifted that I couldn't explain. It wasn't the trophy. It was the feeling that everyone had finally seen who I really was: someone who looks smart until it matters.
When Ms Pillai put up the sign-up sheet for the state round, I walked past it for a week. Vaibhav texted, 'Yamini, sign up with me?' I said I had too many tests. The truth was, if I didn't enter, I couldn't fail again, and nobody would see that version of me.
Vaibhav entered with someone else. They came fourth. I sat in the audience, clapping, feeling smaller than when I'd blanked.

qa.q: How long did Yamini stand silent during the rebuttal?
qa.a: For eight seconds.

qa.q: Why did Yamini avoid the state round sign-up?
qa.a: Yamini feared that failing again would prove being 'someone who looks smart until it matters'; not entering protected that sense of worth.

qa.q: What choice could Yamini make before the next contest, and why?
qa.a: Signing up again, perhaps after talking to Ms Pillai about the blank moment; treating one bad rebuttal as a skill to practise, not a verdict on worth, would loosen the fear.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt entering the state round with someone else?
qa.a: Vaibhav may have felt let down or puzzled by the 'too many tests' excuse, and perhaps worried about Yamini sitting in the audience.

grounding: A teenager who blanked in a debate feels the loss says something about their worth and avoids the next contest.

Debate coach's note, Tuesday. Lavanya.
Charu (Class 10) has not come to practice since losing the inter-house final two weeks ago. Today I found her in the library. She said, very fast, 'I'm just not a debate person. Everyone saw.' Then, quieter: 'If I can't win, what am I even good at?'
That second sentence is the real problem. She isn't afraid of the motion or the other team; she's afraid of what losing says about her.
What I did: I didn't tell her she was brilliant. I showed her the judges' sheet. Her argument scores were the highest in the round; she lost on time management. One fixable skill.
I asked her to keep time for the juniors on Thursday, no speaking. She agreed. It's a start. Next step: a practice round with no audience.

qa.q: What did Charu lose on, according to the judges' sheet?
qa.a: Time management; her argument scores were the highest in the round.

qa.q: What does 'If I can't win, what am I even good at?' reveal about Charu's fear?
qa.a: It shows she feels her worth dropped with the loss; the fear is about what failing says about her, not about debating itself.

qa.q: What choice of Lavanya's might help Charu come back, and why?
qa.a: Showing the judges' sheet and offering a low-stakes job keeping time; it separates one fixable skill from Charu's worth and lets her return without the spotlight.

qa.q: How might the juniors see Charu keeping time on Thursday?
qa.a: They may just see a senior helping out, perhaps one they admire, with no idea of the loss; that ordinary welcome could help Charu feel she still belongs.

'I'm not here to cry,' she said, though her voice shook. 'I wrote down what went wrong, and I want you to check it.'

Shreya, the coordinator, nodded slowly. 'Can I add one? You never asked for help until the end.'

In August she began again with only lime pickle, refillable steel tins and orders through the group. She pinned the sheet to the centre's notice board. Two other women copied it for their own businesses.

qa.a: Only lime pickle, refillable steel tins and orders through the group; each change answered a lesson on her sheet, turning the failure into data for the next try.

qa.a: They seem to see it as useful rather than shameful, a guide they can learn from for their own businesses.

I'm Imran, and in Class 4 I had a trick. When Parveen Ma'am asked a question, I didn't think about the answer. I watched her face.
If I said 'the moon makes its own light' and her eyebrows went up, I'd quickly say, 'I mean, no, it doesn't.' If she smiled, I kept going. My stomach always felt tight while I watched.

In the placement office at the college in Thrissur, Usha stared at two offer letters: one from a firm in Kochi, forty minutes from home, and one from the design studio in Bengaluru she had dreamed about since first year.
'Which one do you want?' asked Imran sir, the placement officer.

qa.q: Why did Usha's eyes fill after she said 'Yes, Appa'?

qa.a: To take a day, decide for herself and then tell her parents why; it lets Usha's own wish count while keeping her family close.

passage:
At the milk cooperative office in a small town near Erode, the clock showed 8 p.m., and Karthik was still sorting the farmers' payment slips for the third village. He'd already covered the morning collection for a colleague and agreed to fix the manager's nephew's computer.
Asif, packing his tiffin, watched him. Karthik said yes to everyone. Last week he'd dozed off at the weighing scale.
'Karthik, go home.'
'Manager asked me. How can I say no?'
Asif sat down beside him. 'Tomorrow, when he asks for the next thing, say you're finishing the slips first. I'll be right there. I'll take the computer.'
Karthik rubbed his eyes. 'He won't think I'm lazy?'
'You? Nobody in this office thinks that.'
Next morning, when the manager came over, Karthik said it, voice shaking a little. The manager just nodded. 'Okay. Finish the slips.'

qa.q: What was Karthik sorting at 8 p.m.?
qa.a: The farmers' payment slips for the third village.

qa.q: Why did Karthik ask 'He won't think I'm lazy?'
qa.a: Karthik worries that saying no would cost him the manager's good opinion; that fear keeps him agreeing to everything.

qa.q: What backup did Asif offer, and why did it help Karthik say no?
qa.a: Being there when the manager asked and taking the computer job; with that support, Karthik could set a limit without fearing he would look lazy.

qa.q: How might the manager see Karthik's first no?
qa.a: The manager simply nodded and told him to finish the slips, suggesting the refusal cost Karthik nothing; the manager may not have known how much Karthik was carrying.

grounding: A colleague notices a man who never says no and is wearing out, and offers backup so he can practise refusing without losing standing.
